claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is uniform and single-phase, with no detectable second phases or grain-boundary segregation.
The initial alloy has high toughness and ductility.
Combined cyclic mechanical loading and moderate temperature fluctuations induce nanoscale chemical ordering at or near grain boundaries.
Local stresses at grain boundaries drive segregation of specific elements.
Stress-induced segregation triggers nanoscale chemical ordering.
Nanoscale chemically ordered grain-boundary regions lower the local energy barrier for brittle intermetallic formation.
Nanoscale ordered regions at or near grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for brittle intermetallic phases.
The resulting brittle intermetallic phases are concentrated at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary intermetallic phases reduce the alloy's capacity to absorb energy and thereby cause embrittlement.
After service-like loading and temperature cycling, the alloy will have lower toughness than its initial single-phase baseline.
The proposed stress-assisted ordering mechanism differs from conventional-alloy embrittlement, which primarily depends on equilibrium grain-boundary segregation.
Moderate cyclic stresses and temperatures can activate local atomic ordering without causing gross grain coarsening.
At substantially higher stresses or temperatures, global microstructural changes such as widespread grain coarsening may become dominant degradation mechanisms.
There are conventional alloys known to embrittle through grain-boundary segregation under conditions comparable to the proposed test.
The stress and temperature thresholds for initiating local chemical ordering are not established.
Sensitivity to the proposed mechanism may differ among high-entropy-alloy compositions.
